title: Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. NRDC (1978)
shortTitle: Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. NRDC (1978)
summary: Courts generally cannot add rulemaking procedures beyond statutory and constitutional requirements; the adequacy of the agency’s substantive explanation remains reviewable.

sections.Parties: Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corporation defended its operating license and the relevant agency rule. The Natural Resources Defense Council and other participants challenged the treatment of nuclear-fuel reprocessing and waste-disposal effects.
sections.Material Facts: The Commission initially excluded fuel-cycle effects from the plant’s individual licensing hearing and later began rulemaking to address them generally. It disclosed a staff environmental survey and background materials, offered alternatives, accepted written and some oral presentations, allowed counsel, questioned presenters, and kept the record open for supplementary statements. It did not allow discovery or cross-examination. The resulting rule supplied numerical environmental values for use in licensing analyses.
sections.Procedural History: The D.C. Circuit set aside the rule because it considered the procedures inadequate despite apparent compliance with § 553, and it remanded the license matter. The Supreme Court rejected that procedural basis and remanded so the court of appeals could assess whether the rule was adequately supported under the APA. The decision did not conclusively approve every substantive aspect of the rule.
sections.Issue: Could a reviewing court require additional adversarial devices because a technically complex and important rulemaking might produce a better record with them? How did that question differ from review of the resulting rule’s support?
sections.Holding: Absent constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances, courts generally may not impose extra rulemaking procedures beyond the applicable statutes. Agencies can choose additional procedures themselves. The appellate court still had to review the justification for the rule under the APA on remand.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court read § 553’s procedural scheme as a congressional settlement that courts could not routinely supplement according to their own preferred process. If agencies had to predict which procedures a court would later consider optimal, they would adopt full trial procedures defensively and lose the advantages Congress preserved for informal rulemaking. Hindsight review of procedure based on the resulting record intensified that pressure. A useful record also need not be identical to a hearing transcript.

The Court distinguished constitutional concerns about narrowly individualized decisions and left open rare issues involving unjustified departures from settled agency procedure. Neither supplied a basis here; NRDC did not maintain a constitutional entitlement to the additional devices in this general rulemaking. The opinion nevertheless preserved substantive review of whether the administrative proceedings justified the rule. Thus failure of support may warrant remand even when the court cannot prescribe a particular evidentiary technique as the solution.

topics.lrs-o-rulemaking-record: The Court rejected tying record adequacy to trial devices while preserving review of whether the rule had sufficient justification.
topics.lrs-o-section-553: Courts generally cannot prescribe extra devices beyond statutory and constitutional requirements, though agencies may choose additional procedures.
topics.lrs-n-hard-look: Vermont Yankee bars judicially imposed procedures while preserving substantive review of the rule's justification, which is the space hard-look review occupies.
